# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains most of the engineering behind a municipal water system. A cubic foot of water weighs about 62.4 pounds, and a column of water only one inch square but ten feet tall already exerts over four pounds of pressure at its base. Every design decision in a city's water infrastructure—from where reservoirs sit to why your shower weakens on a July afternoon—flows from the physics of lifting and holding this heavy fluid.

## The Fundamental Principle: Elevation as Energy

Water systems exploit a beautiful piece of physics: water seeks its own level, and elevation itself stores energy. Engineers talk about "hydraulic head," which is simply the height of water above the point of use. Every foot of elevation provides roughly 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure. If a reservoir sits 200 feet above a faucet, that faucet receives about 87 psi before friction losses—more than enough for typical household needs, which run between 40 and 80 psi.
